How this was made

Both curves hold the amount of practice fixed: the same total number of simulated steps, a fixed-transition budget, however many robots share it. Each training round runs every robot for a short burst, then updates the network once, so more robots means fewer rounds. Each round also carries fixed costs: the learning update, moving data between the graphics chip and the main computer, and the Python loop. The dashed curve adds an assumed cost on the main computer for every robot, which grows with the robot count and flattens the curve.

These are illustrative calculations, not measured training curves: the robot counts, times and the main-computer cost are authored for this lab. The reported Rudin time bounds, their separate protocols and the CPU benchmark that motivates the dashed curve are in the article text. The time axis is logarithmic, from one minute to four hours.

The lab's times along the solid curve: 64 robots, 3.6 hours; 4,096 robots, 4.0 minutes; 16,384 robots, 1.5 minutes. Along the dashed curve: 3.6 hours, 7.3 minutes and 4.8 minutes.

THE 2021 BREAK: PHYSICS MOVED ONTO THE GPU

Isaac Gym kept physics and policy training on one GPU, passing PhysX buffers straight to PyTorch tensors without CPU round trips. Its authors report 2 to 3 orders of magnitude improvement over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU network
Source
3
3 Makoviychuk et al. 2021
, Isaac Gym: High Performance GPU-Based Physics Simulation for Robot Learning
. Viktor Makoviychuk, Lukasz Wawrzyniak, Yunrong Guo et al., 2021
.

Rudin and colleagues scaled from 128 robots, typical of CPU implementations, to 16,384 on one workstation GPU. Flat terrain took under four minutes and uneven terrain twenty, "a speedup of multiple orders of magnitude compared to previous work". Their deployment policy used 4,096 robots, 98,304-transition batches (24 steps per robot) and 1,500 updates in under 20 minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU
Source

WHAT THE ENVIRONMENT COUNT ACTUALLY BUYS

The opening scene is an illustrative calculation: a fixed 220-million-transition budget, an assumed CPU-cost curve that raises per-iteration costs, and a calibrated near-four-minute time at 4,096 environments. Only Rudin's separate deployment run ties 4,096 robots to a reported bound
Source
1
1 Rudin et al. 2021
, Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning
. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist et al., CoRL 2021
.

That curve illustrates a bottleneck the Isaac Lab paper reports: on a state-based Franka drawer task, an RTX 5090 workstation with an AMD 9800X3D nearly matches a server with two RTX PRO 6000 GPUs and two 64-core EPYC 9554 CPUs. The authors attribute this task-dependent result to CPU bottlenecks in PhysX and the training loop, and the workstation's fast single core
Source

LIMITS

GPUSimBench finds GPU batching in Isaac Lab and Genesis adds significant run-to-run and inter-environment variability under identical initial conditions

Isaac Lab targets its CPU bottlenecks in future Isaac Lab and Newton releases. For domain randomization, simulation state sits on the GPU, but mass, friction, contact offsets and joint armature go through PhysX CPU APIs. Mesh scale and collider type change only before simulation starts, most other parameters at runtime

1. RL, Sim-to-Real & Locomotion

Massively Parallel Sim RL

Isaac Lab, Newton, MJX, and Brax: GPU-parallel environments and the wall-clock economics of training.

Updated 17 August 2026 · 8 min read · 33 sources

Contents
  1. Introduction
  2. The 2021 break: physics moved onto the GPU
  3. The JAX line: Brax, MJX, MuJoCo Playground
  4. What the environment count actually buys
  5. Isaac Lab and the framework era
  6. Newton: physics as a multi-solver library
  7. Limits

Massively parallel simulation is training a robot policy across thousands of simulated copies of its environment at once, with the physics on a GPU. It produced Rudin and colleagues' four-minute ANYmal walking runSource 11 Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist et al., CoRL 2021, trained with the 2017 PPOPPOProximal policy optimization, the on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm the locomotion literature standardized on. Schulman and colleagues introduced it as a policy gradient method that alternates between sampling data through interaction with the environment and optimizing a surrogate objective with stochastic gradient ascent, where the surrogate is what allows several epochs of minibatch updates on each batch of samples instead of the single gradient step standard policy gradient takes. It keeps most of trust region policy optimization's reliability without the second-order machinery, and it pairs naturally with massively parallel simulation, where thousands of robots supply the enormous on-policy batches it consumes. algorithmSource 99 Schulman et al. 2017, Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms. John Schulman, Filip Wolski, Prafulla Dhariwal et al., 2017.

Parallel simulation
Running thousands of copies at once speeds training, with limits
Adjust more
training timewith computer overheadrobots shown

beat 2 / 4 4,096 robots at once: 4.0 minutes of training

An illustrative calculation, not a measured training curve

With 4,096 robots side by side on one graphics chip, the same practice finishes in minutes.
How this was made

Both curves hold the amount of practice fixed: the same total number of simulated steps, a fixed-transition budget, however many robots share it. Each training round runs every robot for a short burst, then updates the network once, so more robots means fewer rounds. Each round also carries fixed costs: the learning update, moving data between the graphics chip and the main computer, and the Python loop. The dashed curve adds an assumed cost on the main computer for every robot, which grows with the robot count and flattens the curve.

These are illustrative calculations, not measured training curves: the robot counts, times and the main-computer cost are authored for this lab. The reported Rudin time bounds, their separate protocols and the CPU benchmark that motivates the dashed curve are in the article text. The time axis is logarithmic, from one minute to four hours.

The lab's times along the solid curve: 64 robots, 3.6 hours; 4,096 robots, 4.0 minutes; 16,384 robots, 1.5 minutes. Along the dashed curve: 3.6 hours, 7.3 minutes and 4.8 minutes.

  1. With 64 virtual robots practising at once, the same amount of practice takes hours.
  2. With 4,096 robots side by side on one graphics chip, the same practice finishes in minutes.
  3. Some work for each robot still runs on the main computer, so with that overhead the dashed line flattens.
  4. Robots need huge amounts of practice; a graphics chip running 16,384 virtual robots side by side finishes it in minutes.

The 2021 break: physics moved onto the GPU

Isaac Gym kept physics and policy training on one GPU, passing PhysX buffers straight to PyTorch tensors without CPU round trips. Its authors report 2 to 3 orders of magnitude improvement over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU networkSource 33 Makoviychuk et al. 2021, Isaac Gym: High Performance GPU-Based Physics Simulation for Robot Learning. Viktor Makoviychuk, Lukasz Wawrzyniak, Yunrong Guo et al., 2021.

Rudin and colleagues scaled from 128 robots, typical of CPU implementations, to 16,384 on one workstation GPU. Flat terrain took under four minutes and uneven terrain twenty, "a speedup of multiple orders of magnitude compared to previous work". Their deployment policy used 4,096 robots, 98,304-transition batches (24 steps per robot) and 1,500 updates in under 20 minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPUSource 11 Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist et al., CoRL 2021.

Their game-inspired curriculumcurriculum learningTraining on a scheduled sequence of tasks that grow harder as the agent improves, instead of sampling the full difficulty range from the start. Rudin and colleagues raised or lowered terrain levels based on each robot's progress. Their documented curriculum-trained simulation-and-deployment policy used 4,096 robots, 98,304 transitions per batch and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU; their separate flat-terrain headline is under four minutes on one workstation GPU. promotes robots that cross their tile, demotes those covering under half the commanded distance, and loops hardest-level solvers back to a random levelSource 11 Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist et al., CoRL 2021. The paper's released legged_gym repository (October 2021) is the Isaac Gym environment used to train ANYmal on rough terrain Source 22 Rudin 2021, Isaac Gym Environments for Legged Robots. Nikita Rudin, 2021.

In the massively parallelparallel simulationRunning thousands of physics simulator instances at once on a single GPU, so one workstation collects reinforcement learning experience at rates that once needed CPU clusters. Isaac Gym made the setup practical by keeping both physics and policy training on the GPU and passing data straight from physics buffers to PyTorch tensors, skipping the CPU round-trip entirely, which bought two to three orders of magnitude in throughput over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU learner. Rudin and colleagues showed what that buys: four thousand parallel ANYmal instances trained with PPO learned flat-terrain walking in under four minutes and uneven terrain in twenty, on one workstation GPU. regime, Rudin's PPO also bootstraps the critic at time-outs and adapts the learning rate to a KL target of 0.01Source 11 Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist et al., CoRL 2021.

The JAX line: Brax, MJX, MuJoCo Playground

MuJoCo, a physics engine for model-based controlSource 1010 Todorov et al. 2012, MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control. Emanuel Todorov, Tom Erez, Yuval Tassa, IROS 2012, became free in October 2021 and open source in 2022 under Google DeepMindSource 1111 Google DeepMind 2026, Overview. Google DeepMind, MuJoCo Documentation, as of 2026-10-04. Brax (Google, 2021) compiled physics and learning algorithms in JAX on one accelerator, training performant policies on MuJoCo-like tasks in minutesSource 44 Freeman et al. 2021, Brax: A Differentiable Physics Engine for Large Scale Rigid Body Simulation. C. Daniel Freeman, Erik Frey, Anton Raichuk et al., 2021.

MuJoCo XLA (MJX) ran it on the GPU. MuJoCo Playground (2025) built on it an open framework for quadrupeds, humanoids, hands and arms, with sim-to-real transfer as an express goalSource 55 Zakka et al. 2025, MuJoCo Playground. Kevin Zakka, Baruch Tabanpour, Qiayuan Liao et al., 2025. MJX-Warp, built for NVIDIA GPUs, fixes contact and constraint bottlenecks but lacks automatic differentiationSource 1212 Google DeepMind 2026, MuJoCo XLA (MJX). Google DeepMind, MuJoCo Documentation, as of 2026-10-04. mjlab pairs MuJoCo Warp with Isaac Lab's manager-based APISource 1313 Zakka et al. 2026, mjlab: A Lightweight Framework for GPU-Accelerated Robot Learning. Kevin Zakka, Qiayuan Liao, Brent Yi et al., arXiv preprint, 2026.

What the environment count actually buys

The opening scene is an illustrative calculation: a fixed 220-million-transition budget, an assumed CPU-cost curve that raises per-iteration costs, and a calibrated near-four-minute time at 4,096 environments. Only Rudin's separate deployment run ties 4,096 robots to a reported boundSource 11 Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist et al., CoRL 2021.

That curve illustrates a bottleneck the Isaac Lab paper reports: on a state-based Franka drawer task, an RTX 5090 workstation with an AMD 9800X3D nearly matches a server with two RTX PRO 6000 GPUs and two 64-core EPYC 9554 CPUs. The authors attribute this task-dependent result to CPU bottlenecks in PhysX and the training loop, and the workstation's fast single coreSource 66 NVIDIA et al. 2025, Isaac Lab: A GPU-Accelerated Simulation Framework for Multi-Modal Robot Learning. NVIDIA, Mayank Mittal, Yunrong Guo et al., 2025.

Environment count also changes learning. At fixed batch size, more robots cut Rudin's training time but hurt the policy past a pointSource 11 Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist et al., CoRL 2021. SAPG reports PPO saturating beyond a certain countSource 1414 Singla et al. 2024, SAPG: Split and Aggregate Policy Gradients. Jayesh Singla, Ananye Agarwal, Deepak Pathak, ICML 2024, while Beukman and colleagues avoid plateaus with over 1M environments, improving monotonically to one trillion transitionsSource 1515 Beukman et al. 2026, Preventing Learning Stagnation in PPO by Scaling to 1 Million Parallel Environments. Michael Beukman, Khimya Khetarpal, Zeyu Zheng et al., RLC 2026. Parallel Q-Learning scales off-policy learning to tens of thousands of environmentsSource 1616 Li et al. 2023, Parallel Q-Learning: Scaling Off-policy Reinforcement Learning under Massively Parallel Simulation. Zechu Li, Tao Chen, Zhang-Wei Hong et al., ICML 2023, and FastTD3 solves a range of HumanoidBench tasks in under 3 hours on one A100Source 1717 Seo et al. 2025, FastTD3: Simple, Fast, and Capable Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Control. Younggyo Seo, Carmelo Sferrazza, Haoran Geng et al., arXiv preprint, 2025.

Isaac Lab and the framework era

Isaac Lab grew out of OrbitSource 66 NVIDIA et al. 2025, Isaac Lab: A GPU-Accelerated Simulation Framework for Multi-Modal Robot Learning. NVIDIA, Mayank Mittal, Yunrong Guo et al., 2025, a 2023 framework on Isaac SimSource 1818 Mittal et al. 2023, Orbit: A Unified Simulation Framework for Interactive Robot Learning Environments. Mayank Mittal, Calvin Yu, Qinxi Yu et al., IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 8(6), 2023. Its 2025 paper describes OpenUSD scene graphs, PhysX, RTX rendering, tiled camera rendering in one pass, and Warp ray-cast height scanners and LiDAR-like sensors without photoreal effects. It adds implicit and explicit actuator models, from nonlinear effort limits to learned networks, a manager-based API, and built-in RSL-RL, RL-Games, SKRL, Stable-Baselines3 and RaySource 66 NVIDIA et al. 2025, Isaac Lab: A GPU-Accelerated Simulation Framework for Multi-Modal Robot Learning. NVIDIA, Mayank Mittal, Yunrong Guo et al., 2025.

Headless state-based training on RTX PRO 6000 GPUs scales "almost perfectly linearly". With eight GPUs and 16,384 environments, the DextrAHSource 1919 Lum et al. 2024, DextrAH-G: Pixels-to-Action Dexterous Arm-Hand Grasping with Geometric Fabrics. Tyler Ga Wei Lum, Martin Matak, Viktor Makoviychuk et al., arXiv preprint, 2024 teacher grasp-and-lift task exceeds 900,000 FPS and Franka cabinet 1.6 million, counting environment steps over simulation plus learning timeSource 66 NVIDIA et al. 2025, Isaac Lab: A GPU-Accelerated Simulation Framework for Multi-Modal Robot Learning. NVIDIA, Mayank Mittal, Yunrong Guo et al., 2025.

NVIDIA's 2026 overview says Isaac Lab 3.0 splits backend code from the core API. Users choose Isaac Sim's PhysX and RTX for sensor-rich work or headless Newton for throughput, adding photoreal sensors through the standalone OVRTX renderer, or using Newton's renderer for many-environment vision RLSource 88 Nuñez Cano et al. 2026, The State of Simulation for Physical AI: An Overview. Johnny Nuñez Cano, Mitesh Patel, Asier Arranz et al., 2026. Isaac Lab 3.0 Early Access shipped on 16 September 2026 for Isaac Sim 6.1 and Newton 1.5.2, with general availability targeted for late October 2026Source 2020 NVIDIA 2026, Isaac Lab 3.0 Early Access. NVIDIA, GitHub release v3.0.0-EA, isaac-sim/IsaacLab, 2026.

Newton: physics as a multi-solver library

The Linux Foundation welcomed Newton, an open-source GPU physics engine co-developed by Disney Research, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA, on 29 September 2025Source 2121 The Linux Foundation 2025, Linux Foundation Announces Contribution of Newton by Disney Research, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA to Accelerate Open Robot Learning. The Linux Foundation, Linux Foundation press release, 2025. Newton generalizes the deprecated warp.sim module of NVIDIA Warp, a Python GPU frameworkSource 2222 NVIDIA 2026, NVIDIA Warp. NVIDIA, GitHub repository NVIDIA/warp, README as of 2026-10-04, and uses MuJoCo Warp as its primary backendSource 2323 Foundation) 2026, Newton. Newton project (Linux Foundation), GitHub repository newton-physics/newton, README as of 2026-10-04.

NVIDIA's 16 March 2026 post announced Newton 1.0 GA at GTC 2026, built on Warp and OpenUSD, and called Isaac Sim 6.0 and Isaac Lab 3.0 early access releases Source 77 Reist et al. 2026, Newton Adds Contact-Rich Manipulation and Locomotion Capabilities for Industrial Robotics. Philipp Reist, Miguel Zamora Mora, JC Chang et al., 2026. Isaac Sim 6.1.0 reached general availability on 10 September 2026Source 2424 NVIDIA 2026, Isaac Sim 6.1.0 GA. NVIDIA, GitHub release v6.1.0, isaac-sim/IsaacSim, 2026. Newton v1.6.0 shipped the same day with faster CUDA collision detection, experimental graph-friendly robot controllers and an opt-in compliant mode for the VBD solverSource 2626 Foundation) 2026, Newton v1.6.0. Newton project (Linux Foundation), GitHub release v1.6.0, newton-physics/newton, 2026.

Behind one API, NVIDIA's overview lists MuJoCo and Featherstone solvers in generalized coordinates, and SemiImplicit, XPBD and Kamino in maximal coordinates. VBD (vertex block descentSource 2727 Chen et al. 2024, Vertex Block Descent. Anka He Chen, Ziheng Liu, Yin Yang et al., arXiv preprint, 2024) handles rigid bodies, particles, cloth and soft bodies with limited joints, implicit MPM particle-based continuum materials, and Style3D clothSource 88 Nuñez Cano et al. 2026, The State of Simulation for Physical AI: An Overview. Johnny Nuñez Cano, Mitesh Patel, Asier Arranz et al., 2026. The release post credits Disney Research's Kamino with closed-chain mechanisms and describes coupling VBD and MPM with MuJoCo Warp for deformable manipulation and locomotionSource 77 Reist et al. 2026, Newton Adds Contact-Rich Manipulation and Locomotion Capabilities for Industrial Robotics. Philipp Reist, Miguel Zamora Mora, JC Chang et al., 2026.

The post describes SDF collision from CAD meshes and Drake-inspired hydroelastic contact over finite-area patches, and its assembly example sets a plus or minus 10 mm sparse-SDF band, narrow_band_range=(-0.01, 0.01) Source 77 Reist et al. 2026, Newton Adds Contact-Rich Manipulation and Locomotion Capabilities for Industrial Robotics. Philipp Reist, Miguel Zamora Mora, JC Chang et al., 2026. Isaac Sim 6.1 added hydroelastic contact, a pressure-field modelSource 2828 Elandt et al. 2019, A pressure field model for fast, robust approximation of net contact force and moment between nominally rigid objects. Ryan Elandt, Evan Drumwright, Michael Sherman et al., IROS 2019, to its experimental Newton integrationSource 2525 NVIDIA 2026, Isaac Sim 6.1.0 Release Notes. NVIDIA, Isaac Sim documentation, 2026.

NVIDIA reports that Skild AI trains GPU-rack-assembly RL policies, including connector insertion, with Isaac Lab's Newton backend, SDF and hydroelastic contact. It says Samsung "will use Newton" for synthetic VLA training data and that Lightwheel tunes SimReady assets on real measurements. Its refrigerator example couples MuJoCo Warp two-way with a VBD cable solver for RB-Y1 cable insertion, and mentions a water-hose connector insertionSource 77 Reist et al. 2026, Newton Adds Contact-Rich Manipulation and Locomotion Capabilities for Industrial Robotics. Philipp Reist, Miguel Zamora Mora, JC Chang et al., 2026.

NVIDIA also reports MuJoCo 3.5 (MJWarp) speedups over MJX of 252x for locomotion and 475x for manipulation on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, without stating task variants, environment counts, precision or timing definitionSource 77 Reist et al. 2026, Newton Adds Contact-Rich Manipulation and Locomotion Capabilities for Industrial Robotics. Philipp Reist, Miguel Zamora Mora, JC Chang et al., 2026. MJWarp optimizes throughput, where MuJoCo optimizes single-step latencySource 2929 Google DeepMind et al. 2026, MuJoCo Warp (MJWarp). Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, MuJoCo Documentation, as of 2026-10-04.

Limits

GPUSimBench finds GPU batching in Isaac Lab and Genesis adds significant run-to-run and inter-environment variability under identical initial conditionsSource 3030 Zhang et al. 2026, GPUSimBench: Towards Scalable and Reliable GPU-Accelerated Simulators in Embodied AI. Huzhenyu Zhang, Shenghai Yuan, Wenrui Yan et al., IROS 2026.

Isaac Lab targets its CPU bottlenecks in future Isaac Lab and Newton releases. For domain randomizationdomain randomizationTraining a policy across a distribution of simulators with randomized parameters, visual appearance, dynamics, or both, so the real world reads as one more sample from that distribution. Tobin et al. randomized rendering and transferred an object detector to a real arm; Peng et al. randomized dynamics and transferred a pushing policy with no real-world training. The price is conservatism: a policy that does well across a wide distribution is optimal for no single instance of it., simulation state sits on the GPU, but mass, friction, contact offsets and joint armature go through PhysX CPU APIs. Mesh scale and collider type change only before simulation starts, most other parameters at runtimeSource 66 NVIDIA et al. 2025, Isaac Lab: A GPU-Accelerated Simulation Framework for Multi-Modal Robot Learning. NVIDIA, Mayank Mittal, Yunrong Guo et al., 2025.

Newton's README lists differentiabilitySource 2323 Foundation) 2026, Newton. Newton project (Linux Foundation), GitHub repository newton-physics/newton, README as of 2026-10-04, and support differs between solvers Source 88 Nuñez Cano et al. 2026, The State of Simulation for Physical AI: An Overview. Johnny Nuñez Cano, Mitesh Patel, Asier Arranz et al., 2026. Its primary backend states: "Differentiability via Warp is not yet available"Source 3131 Google DeepMind et al. 2026, MuJoCo Warp (MJWarp). Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, GitHub repository google-deepmind/mujoco_warp, README as of 2026-10-04. SHAC cut training time over 17x against the best established RL algorithm on muscle-actuated locomotionSource 3232 Xu et al. 2022, Accelerated Policy Learning with Parallel Differentiable Simulation. Jie Xu, Viktor Makoviychuk, Yashraj Narang et al., ICLR 2022. Schwarke and colleagues report the first legged sim-to-real transfer learned entirely in differentiable simulationSource 3333 Schwarke et al. 2024, Learning Deployable Locomotion Control via Differentiable Simulation. Clemens Schwarke, Victor Klemm, Joshua Bagajo et al., arXiv preprint (CoRL 2025), 2024.

Isaac Sim 6.1 adds beta system identificationsystem identificationMeasuring a real robot's dynamics and correcting the simulator's parameters to match, so the sim-to-real gap shrinks by calibration rather than by randomization. Hwangbo and colleagues replaced a miscalibrated analytic actuator model with a learned network mapping joint-command history to realized torque after identifying actuator error as the dominant transfer obstacle on ANYmal. The method attacks the dynamics component of the gap directly, where domain randomization only averages over it. tools for headless and interactive optimization of robot simulation parametersSource 2525 NVIDIA 2026, Isaac Sim 6.1.0 Release Notes. NVIDIA, Isaac Sim documentation, 2026. The overview's authors call Drake the "gold standard" when contact-implicit trajectory optimisation and rigorous numerics matter more than throughputSource 88 Nuñez Cano et al. 2026, The State of Simulation for Physical AI: An Overview. Johnny Nuñez Cano, Mitesh Patel, Asier Arranz et al., 2026.
